10.1002/adfm.79042.abstract: ABSTRACT The regeneration of graphite anodes from spent lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) is essential for sustainable battery recycling. Existing strategies typically rely on energy‐intensive graphitization or hazardous chemical treatments, which are either ineffective in repairing intrinsic defects or environmentally unsustainable. Here, we show that spent graphite largely retains its graphitic framework and therefore requires selective healing of localized defects and removal of surface residues, rather than complete structural reconstruction. We develop an ultrafast thermal strategy using flash Joule heating (2273 K within 0.1 s, held for 10 s), which simultaneously repairs lattice defects and removes surface residues with minimal thermal budget. Moreover, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are integrated into graphite and ultrafast thermal treatment enables interfacial fusion between CNTs and graphite domains, reconstructing long‐range conductive pathways across particles. This process transforms CNTs from passive conductive additives into active structural reconstruction agents. As a result, the regenerated graphite exhibits enhanced structural integrity and electron transport, delivering superior rate capability, cycling stability, and low‐temperature performance. In addition, the process suppresses thermal‐shock‐induced powder loss and significantly reduces energy consumption. This work establishes a mechanism‐driven strategy for defect‐selective healing and conductive‐network reconstruction in spent graphite, providing a promising and sustainable pathway for lithium‐ion battery recycling.

10.1002/adma.74297.abstract: Near-critical thinning turns porous polyethylene from a hydrophobic, electrically insulating barrier into a thickness-gated membrane electrode. As the membrane approaches ∼60 nm, blocked mass and electron transport become accessible without changing chemistry, enabling hydrophobic-yet-permeable, electronically addressable polymer interfaces for liquid-phase electrochemical conversion. ABSTRACT Electrochemical systems are constrained by a materials paradox: chemically robust porous separators are typically hydrophobic and electronically insulating, forcing bulky, carbon-rich interfaces to couple mass transport and electrical contact. Here we show that pushing freestanding porous polyethylene into a near-critical ultrathin regime turns thickness into a geometric gate, enabling these functions to be switched without chemical modification. Near an inferred lower bound (∼10 nm), a 60 nm membrane already enters this regime: liquid-entry pressure collapses into a sub-bar window, enabling aqueous-electrolyte permeation, while the electrical threshold shifts to sub-volt soft dielectric breakdown, yielding persistent through-plane conductivity. The same scaffold enhances nanowire-matrix coupling via high conformability and real contact area, enabling a binder- and carbon-free ∼300 nm ultrathin membrane electrode. As a stringent liquid-phase electrochemical validation, this membrane electrode drives selective nitrate-to-ammonia electroreduction in flowing alkaline electrolytes with sustained performance. Near-critical ultrathinness thus emerges as a gateable design dimension for re-imagining commodity plastics as transmembrane-active platforms.

10.1002/adma.74572.abstract: Thermal nitrate decomposition drives an inside-out multiscale reconstruction of Ni-rich cathodes. By integrating a stress-buffering central pore, a strain-retardant perovskite phase, and a protective surface layer, this architecture synchronizes chemomechanical stabilization and Li + transport. The resulting cathode suppresses oxygen evolution and microcracking, delivering outstanding stability and rate capability under high-voltage and elevated-temperature conditions. ABSTRACT Ni-rich layered oxides (LiNi x Co y Mn 1− x − y O 2 , x ≥ 0.8) are indispensable for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries, yet they suffer from severe chemomechanical degradation driven by the synergy of internal microcracking and interfacial parasitic side reactions. Existing strategies inherently suffer from decoupled regulation of mechanical and chemical instabilities that fail to address these issues holistically. Here, we develop an inside-out structural reconfiguration strategy driven by the thermal decomposition of nitrates, concurrently tailoring the core, bulk, and surface of NCM811 in a single calcination step. This reconstruction generates a stress-buffering central pore architecture that effectively homogenizes anisotropic lattice strain and suppresses crack nucleation. Concurrently, the regulated Nd 3+ diffusion forms a coherent Nd 4 [LiNi]O 8 (NLNO) perovskite phase within the bulk lattice, creating a pinning effect that stabilizes the layered framework and enhances charge transport. Furthermore, excess Nd-species evolve into a conformal NLNO surface coating, acting as a physical barrier and oxygen reservoir to resist electrolyte attack and oxygen evolution. The modified cathode delivers an exceptional capacity retention (95.7% after 200 cycles at 4.5 V) and exceptional rate capability (157.1 mAh g −1 at 5 C). Even under stringent conditions (4.6 V or 45°C), a superior retention of 87.8% is maintained after 200 cycles, demonstrating remarkable chemomechanical robustness.

10.1002/adma.74714.abstract: This work proposes a cross-scale strategy to construct Cu/MoS 2 nanoreactor consisting of hollow MoS 2 loaded with Cu single atoms and clusters. Its heat-exchanger-fin-like structure and dual-species spillover effect break mass-transfer and energy-barrier bottlenecks for boosted nitrate-to-ammonia reduction. In real wastewater, the assembled Al-NO 3 − battery achieves stable power generation, efficient nitrate removal, and ammonia electrosynthesis. ABSTRACT Copper-based materials are promising catalysts for electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (NH 3 ), while their use in real wastewater with low nitrate concentrations is hindered by poor mass transfer and high energy barrier. To overcome these limitations, we design a hollow Cu/MoS 2 -550 nanoreactor, consisting of hollow MoS 2 support loaded with Cu single atoms and clusters. At the mesoscale, the hollow MoS 2 support features a heat-exchanger-fin-like structure that accelerates mass transfer, thereby promoting local enrichment of NO 3 − . At the microscale, precise modulation of sulfur vacancy concentration in MoS 2 triggers dual-species spillover, namely reverse hydrogen spillover and *NO spillover from Cu single atoms to Cu clusters, which lowers the energy barrier of deep hydrogenation step. As a result, the Cu/MoS 2 -550 nanoreactor achieves an NH 3 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 98.14% and a yield rate of 27.46 mg h −1 mg cat −1 . Furthermore, when assembled into an Al-NO 3 − battery operating in real wastewater containing only ∼ 0.76 mM NO 3 − , the battery runs stably for 120 h, delivers an NH 3 FE of 53.20%, and maintains a nitrate removal rate of 91.17%. This work provides cross-scale modulation strategies to overcome mass-transfer bottlenecks and energy barriers in multi-electron transfer reactions, offering a potential pathway for environmental applications.

10.1002/adma.74943.abstract: A p-type tetraazanaphthotetraphene ligand enables precise control over single-atom Ni sites in a hollow conductive MOF, accelerating proton transfer and hydrogenation kinetics for electrocatalytic NO reduction. This strategy delivers exceptional ammonia production and enables a Zn-NO battery with 2.1 mW cm −2 power density. ABSTRACT Electrochemical reduction of ammonia represents a highly promising approach for transforming harmful environmental pollutants into more valuable products. In this study, we successfully achieved precise control over the environment surrounding single-atom Ni sites by modifying functional groups on ligands. To validate this strategy, we constructed two similar hollow Ni-MOFs. The metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) containing the p-type tetraazanaphthotetraphene ligand (Ni-TT) demonstrated exceptional performance compared to n-type triphenylene (Ni-TP). Its overall reduction rate reached 196.9 µmol·h −1 ·cm 2 , with a Faraday efficiency as high as 90.9% at −0.4 V versus RHE. The exceptional performance of Ni-TT stems from the p-type tetranaphthalenetetracene ligand, which is nitrogen-rich and electron-deficient. The electronic properties of the ligand significantly influence the coordination environment around the single-atom Ni site, enabling precise control over proton-transfer behavior during the reaction. Theoretical calculations also indicate that hydrogen adsorption on p-type Ni-TT surfaces accelerates hydrogen transfer at Ni active sites compared to n-type Ni-TP. This significantly enhances the rate-determining step (RDS) in the NO hydrogenation process. The constructed Ni-TT-based Zn-NO battery achieved a power density of 2.1 mW cm −2 . These results provide insight into how conjugated ligand structures modulate the electronic structure and hydrogenation behavior, which may guide future studies on MOF-based electrocatalysts for nitric oxide reduction reaction (NORR).

10.1002/adma.75456.abstract: Metal–organic framework-derived Co 3 O 4 (MD-Co 3 O 4 ) features oxygen-vacancies that selectively reconstruct octahedral cobalt (CoOh) sites into an electron-rich, high-spin state. The resulting CoOh centers strengthen nitrate adsorption and accelerate its conversion to ammonia, delivering a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 96.7% along with superior stability and broad applicability. ABSTRACT Ammonia is vital for agriculture and a promising carbon-free energy carrier, but its industrial production via the Haber–Bosch process is energy-intensive and emits substantial CO 2 . Electrocatalytic nitrogen oxide reduction to ammonia offers a green alternative, by using renewable electricity under ambient conditions while enabling nitrogen resource utilization. Herein, we report a metal–organic framework (MOF)-derived Co 3 O 4 electrocatalyst (MD-Co 3 O 4 ) prepared by controlled pyrolysis of Co-MOF-74, which achieved a high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 96.7% and excellent stability for the electrosynthesis of NH 3 from nitrate, along with robust activity over a wide pH and nitrate concentration range. Comprehensive spectroscopic characterizations and density functional theory calculations revealed that the oxygen vacancies generated during MOF pyrolysis induce coordination distortion of octahedral Co sites, leading to a high-spin state transition with an electron-rich configuration that synergistically enhances nitrate adsorption and interfacial electron transfer, thereby boosting the intrinsic activity. Moreover, this MOF-based strategy is applicable to other M 1 Co 2 O 4 spinels, which provides an effective approach for spin engineering at the atomic scale and sustainable ammonia synthesis.

10.1002/adma.75462.abstract: A Co/Co 7 Fe 3 heterostructure is designed to drive electrocatalytic nitrate reduction via a unique [4+4] tandem mechanism. The interfacial electric field modulates the local water network, accelerates water dissociation, and enables hydrogen spillover. Its heterointerfaces optimize the adsorption energetics of key intermediates, and its synergistic dual spillover enhances the reaction, delivering a high NH 3 yield rate with nearly 100% Faradaic efficiency. ABSTRACT Rational design of dual-site catalysts to decouple complex multi-electron pathways is crucial for efficient electrocatalytic nitrate (NO 3 − ) reduction reaction (NO 3 RR). Here, we construct a Co/Co 7 Fe 3 heterojunction with strong electronic coupling that drives NO 3 RR efficiently via an unconventional [4+4] tandem mechanism. In this [4+4] pathway, the first 4-electron step reduces NO 3 − to the *HNOH intermediate at the Fe sites. The second 4-electron process involves the migration of *HNOH to adjacent Co sites, followed by a 4-electron hydrogenation step. Experimental and theoretical investigations demonstrate that the interfacial electric field modulates the local water network, accelerating water dissociation and ensuring a robust proton supply via hydrogen spillover. Benefiting from well-defined heterointerfaces, the adsorption energetics of key intermediates are favorably optimized, endowing Co/Co 7 Fe 3 with markedly boosted electrocatalytic activity for NO 3 RR through synergistic dual-spillover effects, and enabling it to achieve a near-unity Faradaic efficiency of 99.16% ± 0.3% and a remarkable NH 3 yield rate of 36.07 ± 0.52 mg h −1 cm −2 at −0.48 V versus RHE. Additionally, a rechargeable Zn-nitrate battery featuring this material as the cathode delivers a peak power density of 18.15 mW cm −2 with excellent cycling stability. This study provides a novel paradigm for designing efficient tandem electrocatalysts.

10.1002/admi.70704.abstract: ABSTRACT 2D transition‐metal carbides and nitrides, known as MXenes, have emerged as promising electrocatalysts for nitrogen‐related reactions, including ammonia oxidation (AOR), nitrogen reduction (NRR), and nitrate reduction (NO 3 RR). Their appeal stems from a layered architecture, abundant active sites, tunable surface chemistry, and high electrical conductivity. Key physicochemical properties—including controllable surface terminations (–O, –OH, –F), defect‐rich surfaces, and flexible electronic structures—facilitate intermediate adsorption and activation while enhancing charge‐transfer kinetics. Recent synthesis methods, such as HF etching and fluorine‐free Lewis acid approaches, enable precise control over functionalities that dictate catalytic performance. Furthermore, engineering strategies like heteroatom doping, defect engineering, and hybrid composite formation are explored to optimize activity, selectivity, and durability. Ti 3 C 2 T X remains the most extensively studied platform due to its versatility and performance. This review provides a comprehensive overview of advancements in MXene‐based catalysts for NO 3 RR, NRR, and AOR, highlighting the relationships between reaction mechanisms, electronic structures, and synthesis strategies. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives for the rational design of efficient, scalable, and sustainable MXene catalysts for nitrogen‐related energy applications are discussed.

10.1002/ange.3369650.abstract: ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic nitric oxide reduction to ammonia (NORR) offers a dual opportunity for NO remediation and decentralized NH 3 production, yet its efficiency is often limited by competing pathways and unclear structure–function relationships. Here we introduce a reactant‐shunting strategy that installs a guiding electrocatalytic step via isolated Ru atoms to supply surface‐bound * H species and enforce a Langmuir–Hinshelwood (LH) hydrogenation pathway. Using Ru 1 /Co 3 O 4 as a model catalyst, we show that single Ru sites promote water adsorption and dissociation, forming stable Ru‐H intermediates that thermodynamically and kinetically accelerate the coupling‐hydrogenation steps in NORR. The optimized catalyst delivers an NH 3 yield of 533.49 µmol cm −2 h −1 with a 97.19% faradaic efficiency, surpassing state‐of‐the‐art systems. The reactant‐shunting principle further generalizes across multiple oxide hosts, enhancing NH 3 productivity by up to threefold. These findings establish pathway steering through controlled hydrogen delivery as a powerful strategy for high‐efficiency electrocatalytic ammonia synthesis.

10.1002/anie.1513379.abstract: A Janus CuN 3 –PdS 3 dual-atom catalyst on N/S co-doped carbon (CuPd-SNC) spatially decouples nitrate adsorption/activation from hydrogen supply during electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR). The Cu sites activate NO x intermediates, Pd sites provide reactive hydrogen, and N/S bridges mediate *H spillover, enabling 99.58% Faradaic efficiency for ammonia synthesis and stable Zn–nitrate battery operation. ABSTRACT Electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) using renewable electricity offers a carbon-free and energy-saving route to remediating nitrate-polluted wastewater while producing ammonia (NH 3 ). However, conventional catalysts for NO 3 RR suffer from strong adsorption of NO x intermediates that hinders further hydrogenation, resulting in diminished selectivity and catalyst deactivation. Here we construct a Janus-type CuN 3 −PdS 3 dual-atom catalyst featuring N/S dual bridging, namely CuPd-SNC, to enable decoupled NO x species adsorption and hydrogen supply for hydrogenation on Cu and Pd sites, respectively. Excitingly, CuPd-SNC delivers a near-unity Faradaic efficiency of 99.58% for NH 3 synthesis and a production rate of 1.34 mmol h −1 cm −2 . When integrated into a Zn–nitrate battery, CuPd-SNC achieves a maximum power density of 13.0 mW cm −2 and demonstrates stable operation for >160 h. In situ spectroscopic and theoretical analyses reveal the site-specific functionalities of the CuN 3 −PdS 3 Janus configuration, wherein Cu sites markedly enhance the adsorption/activation of NO x − intermediates, Pd sites enable continuous proton supply and reduce the energy barriers for multi-step *NO x hydrogenation, while N/S dual bridges serve as a proton reservoir. These findings highlight the site-specific but complementary functioning of dual-atom catalysts in synergistically pushing the limit of conventional electrocatalysts, offering fundamental insights into the rational catalyst design for NH 3 synthesis.

10.1002/anie.1879497.abstract: Ammonia decomposition catalyzed by base metals: Exsolution of cobalt from perovskites prepared by spray-flame synthesis (SFS) yields highly active, SrO-promoted Co/La 2 O 3 catalysts with low cobalt content. Operando studies provide insight into the function of the promoter. Dynamic surface reconstruction under operating conditions increases the interface between SrO and Co and prevents the blocking of active Co sites by mobile La-containing species. ABSTRACT Storing energy in molecular form, particularly hydrogen in carbon-free carriers such as ammonia, is considered a key strategy for future energy systems. The release of hydrogen via ammonia decomposition is a critical step in this context that requires scalable and economically viable catalysts. In this work, spray-flame synthesis (SFS) was employed to prepare La 1– x Sr x CoO 3− δ (0≤ x ≤ 1) nanoparticles (≈ 10 nm), which serve as precursors for SrO-promoted Co/La 2 O 3 catalysts prepared by exsolution. ESR, operando XRD, and ambient pressure photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS) provide insights into dynamic interfacial restructuring of the catalysts under the harsh ammonia decomposition conditions. The catalysts contain 25 wt% Co and achieve a maximum hydrogen productivity of 108 mmolH2${\mathrm{mmo}}{{\mathrm{l}}_{{{\mathrm{H}}_{\mathrm{2}}}}}$·g Co −1 ·min −1 at 500°C for the La 0.75 Sr 0.25 CoO 3− δ -derived material. The coverage of La 2 O 3 with SrO/Sr─OH species under reaction conditions inhibits the migration of La-based species, which block active Co sites in the absence of the promoter. An excess of Sr, however, promotes the growth of Co particles and reduces the exposed Co surface area. Beyond its structural role, operando APXPS reveals that SrO also influences reaction kinetics by facilitating NH x decomposition and weakening the binding strength of nitrogen, which is consistent with an electrostatic effect of SrO.

10.1002/anie.3154221.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (eNO 3 RR) offers a sustainable route for nitrate removal and nitrogen valorization, yet its selectivity is governed by complex intermediate evolution. This Review focuses on intermediate behaviors in eNO 3 RR, covering their transformation pathways, detection methods, and regulation strategies. By linking mechanistic insights with catalyst and interfacial design, it highlights opportunities to steer nitrate conversion toward NH 3 , N 2 , or NH 2 OH. ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic nitrate (NO 3 − ) reduction reaction (eNO 3 RR) has emerged as a promising strategy for waste NO 3 − valorization, offering opportunities for environmental remediation. However, its complex proton-coupled electron transfer processes involve multiple competing pathways, in which the fate of key intermediates governs reaction activity and product selectivity. In this review, we provide an intermediate-centered perspective on eNO 3 RR, covering the reaction pathways from NO 3 − activation to the selective synthesis of NH 3 , N 2 , and NH 2 OH. We then summarize current techniques for probing N-containing intermediates and active hydrogen (*H). On this basis, we discuss how catalyst design and microenvironment engineering regulate key processes in eNO 3 RR, including intermediate adsorption, retention and desorption, N─O bond cleavage, hydrogenation, and N─N coupling. We also examine the emerging role of data-driven approaches in optimizing eNO 3 RR systems. Drawing these discussions together, we distill principles for selective product synthesis. Finally, we discuss remaining challenges in achieving a deeper mechanistic understanding, regulating the interfacial microenvironment, and applying eNO 3 RR to real wastewater.

10.1002/anie.3649572.abstract: We demonstrate that a dynamic asymmetry in the O/N-coordinated Zn single-atom catalysts promotes Sabatier-favorable urea and H 2 O 2 electrosynthesis, enabling subsequent urea peroxide production. ABSTRACT Precise regulation of metal‒intermediate binding is essential for selective electrocatalysis, yet conventional symmetric single-atom coordination often limits directional adsorption control. Here we report an asymmetric O/N-co-coordinated Zn single-atom catalyst, Zn-O 3 N 1 -C, using symmetric Zn-O 4 -C as a structural counterpart. Structural characterization and x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) confirm atomically dispersed Zn‒O 3 N 1 sites, in which replacing one O ligand with less electronegative N not only breaks local symmetry, but also enriches Zn electron density and lowers the Zn oxidation state. Operando XAS further reveals that Zn–O 3 N 1 undergoes cathodic-bias-induced electronic enrichment and anisotropic Zn─N/Zn─O bond response, amplifying local coordination polarization while preserving the isolated Zn─O/N framework. This dynamically polarized asymmetric coordination shifts Zn‒adsorbate interactions toward a Sabatier-favorable regime, enabling two adsorption-governed transformations. For CO 2 /nitrate co-reduction, Zn-O 3 N 1 -C promotes *NO/*NHO-mediated C‒N coupling. The same catalyst also demonstrates excellent electrocatalytic activity toward two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e − ORR). The electrosynthesized urea and H 2 O 2 are further coupled to produce urea peroxide. Operando spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal that asymmetric Zn–O 3 N 1 coordination optimizes *NO/*NHO and *OOH binding, establishing dynamic coordination polarization as a design principle for selective single-atom electrocatalysis.

10.1002/anie.3793785.abstract: We have developed a series of Cu 1 /M 1 -NOC dual-atom electrocatalysts for electrochemical urea synthesis via CO 2 and NO 3 − /NO 2 − co-reduction. The modulation of metal sites switches *CO adsorption configuration from bridge-bound to linear-bound (*CO L ), and the electrophilic *CO L greatly facilitates coupling with N-intermediates beneficial for C─N formation. The optimal Cu 1 /M 1 -NOC achieves 73.73% and 67.3% urea Faradaic efficiency with NO 2 − and NO 3 − , respectively. ABSTRACT Electrochemical urea synthesis through CO 2 and nitrate/nitrite (NO 3 − /NO 2 − ) co-reduction represents a revolutionary alternative pathway for urea formation. Although studies reveal that restraining C-intermediates desorption is beneficial for C-N coupling, *CO adsorption behaviors were usually described by *CO binding energy based on DFT calculations. The intrinsic reason why the *CO adsorption behaviors could modulate the activity for urea formation remains ambiguous. Herein, a series of high-density Cu 1 /M 1 -NOC electrocatalysts regarding single-atomically dispersed Cu 1 /Cu 1 , Cu 1 /Ni 1 , Cu 1 /Au 1 , or Cu 1 /Pd 1 sites anchored on N, O-co-doped carbon were developed for electrochemical urea synthesis. In situ spectroscopy reveals that strengthening *CO binding energy not only enhances *CO coverage but also increases the proportion of linear *CO absorption configuration (*CO L ). The *CO L with sp hybridization exhibits stronger electrophilicity than that for bridge adsorption, thereby favoring coupling with N-intermediates. Notably, a linear relationship was established by plotting urea yield versus *CO L coverage. As such, the intrinsic reason for facilitating C─N coupling was originated from the local enrichment of *CO L . The optimal Cu 1 /Pd 1 -NOC catalyst exhibits the high urea Faradaic efficiencies of 73.73% and 67.3% with NO 2 − and NO 3 − as N source, respectively. This research provides an effective strategy to boost urea performance by precisely controlling the *CO adsorption behaviors.

10.1002/anie.7739547.abstract: Hard Lewis acid Mo 6+ induces N-end adsorption of urea to steer selective nitrite electrosynthesis. Directional electron redistribution generates a polarized surface that stabilizes configuration-selective adsorption, promotes C─N bond cleavage, and suppresses competing pathways, enabling efficient nitrogen upgrading from wastewater. ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic urea oxidation reaction (UOR) offers a promising route for coupling wastewater remediation with nitrogen upgrading. However, the structural complexity of urea, containing both electron-donating (─NH 2 ) and electron-withdrawing (C = O) groups, leads to multiple adsorption configurations, resulting in poorly defined pathways and low selectivity toward nitrite (NO 2 ‾ ). Here, guided by Pearson's hard-soft acid-base theory, we develop a hard Lewis acid strategy by incorporating Mo 6+ into NiCo layered double hydroxide (NiCoMo-LDH) to regulate interfacial electronic structure. The strong electron-accepting nature of Mo 6+ regulates the electronic environment of Ni/Co centers, facilitating the formation and stabilization of high-valent NiOOH/CoOOH species while creating polarized interfacial sites with enhanced affinity toward urea activation. Importantly, Mo-induced modulation does not merely increase oxidative capability; instead, it introduces substrate-specific adsorption regulation that favors UOR over the competing OER. This configuration regulation facilitates selective C-N bond cleavage of the *NCONH 2 intermediate and subsequent oxidation of the generated nitrogen species toward NO 2 ‾ , achieving a Faradaic efficiency of 93.4% and a production rate of 1732.7 µmol h −1 cm −2 . This work establishes Lewis acid modulation as a strategy for controlling adsorption configurations and steering selective electrosynthesis.

10.1002/anie.8178911.abstract: CO 2 is not merely a mineralization product: at reduced quinone sites, it forms carbonate adducts that poison 2e − oxygen reduction. A redox-gated pulsed electrocatalysis strategy periodically reoxidizes quinone sites to release bound CO 2 in situ, boosting degradation kinetics and sustaining metal-free electrocatalytic water purification. ABSTRACT Quinone-based metal-free electrocatalysts offer a sustainable route for oxygen activation and water purification, yet their persistent activity decay has remained poorly understood. Here, we identify mineralization-derived CO 2 as the major cause of a previously overlooked self-poisoning pathway in quinone‑based electrocatalysts: CO 2 accumulates at the electrode–electrolyte interface and forms stable carbonate adducts with reduced quinone moieties, blocking the active sites for two-electron oxygen reduction to H 2 O 2 and consequently suppressing ·OH generation through the cascade oxygen-reduction pathway. Electrochemical analysis further reveals that CO 2 adduction reorganizes the native quinone redox transitions into potential-dependent carbonate-bound states, allowing the occupied quinone centers to be reversibly regenerated by oxidative pulses. Leveraging this principle, we developed a pulsed electrocatalytic strategy that periodically reoxidizes the quinone catalyst in situ, dynamically reversing CO 2 poisoning without requiring chemical regenerants or thermal treatment. Across structurally diverse pollutants at neutral pH, this strategy accelerates degradation kinetics by up to 725.3% and retains up to 93.6% of its 2 h diclofenac removal efficiency after 12 h of continuous operation. More broadly, the redox-gated CO 2 switching mechanism provides a generalizable design paradigm for mitigating CO 2 -induced deactivation in electrocatalytic systems prone to local CO 2 buildup, including CO 2 electrolysis, electrosynthetic biomass conversion, and electrochemical nitrogen fixation.

10.1002/anie.9113894.abstract: A molecular–atomic dual active centers catalyst is constructed to create a homo/heterogeneous interface, where carbon and nitrogen activation are spatially separated yet kinetically synchronized, ensuring a sustained supply of *CO and *NO intermediates. Their convergence and subsequent coupling through a *NOCO intermediate direct selective formamide formation, establishing a general design principle for electrocatalytic C─N bond construction. ABSTRACT Electrochemical C─N coupling from carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxoanions offers a sustainable route to value-added amides, yet achieving high selectivity remains challenging due to competing reaction pathways and insufficient substrate activation. Here we report a homo/heterogeneous dual-active-center catalyst that integrates molecular copper phthalocyanine with atomically dispersed chromium sites on porous carbon nanospheres to enable selective electrosynthesis of formamide under neutral conditions. The molecular Cu centers selectively reduce CO 2 to CO, while Cr single atoms promote nitrate (NO 3 − ) and nitrite (NO 2 − ) activation to *NO intermediates, furnishing spatially separated yet kinetically matched reactive species. As a result, the catalyst achieves a formamide faradaic efficiency (FE) of 35.2% from CO 2 and NO 3 – , increasing to 44.9% using NO 2 − , with high stability and activity even at low NO 3 − concentrations. In situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal *NO─CO coupling via a *NOCO intermediate as the key pathway. ABSTRACT Iron parent imides serve as key intermediates for iron-promoted nitrogen fixation and ammonia oxidation. However, these active species are difficult to be isolated, and their reactivities are underexplored. So far, only a few multinuclear iron parent imides were reported, but none plays a key intersection during the bidirectional transformation. Herein, we adopt the bulky 1,2,4-tri( tert -butyl)cyclopentadienyl (Cp′) and bidentate 1,3-propanedithiolate (pdt) ligand to provide the steric protection for the reactive [Fe 2 S 2 ] scaffold. As predicted, the highly active imido species can be captured by this [Fe 2 S 2 ] platform to generate a novel thiolate-bridged diiron parent μ -imide complex 3 . Mössbauer spectroscopy and DFT calculation reveal that 3 features a bent {Fe III −NH 2− −Fe III } framework with two anti-ferromagnetic coupled, low-spin Fe(III) centers. Importantly, imide 3 can not only undergo protonation to generate amide and finally release ammonia, but also go through hydrogen atom transfer to regenerate nitride. This reactivity indicates that 3 is a key junction that associates the late stage (N 3− → NH 2− → NH 2 − → NH 3 ) of nitrogen fixation and the initial period (NH 2 − → NH 2− → N 3− ) of ammonia oxidation. Overall, this work provides one available strategy that can stabilize a high-activity imide and investigate its reactivity of bidirectional interconversion.

10.1002/cctc.71109.abstract: ABSTRACT Global ammonia production is dominated by the energy‐intensive Haber‐Bosch process, motivating the development of sustainable electrochemical alternatives. While lithium‐ and calcium‐mediated systems in organic solvents have relatively high yields, aqueous electrochemical nitrogen reduction (N 2 ER) remains inefficient. Density functional theory (DFT) studies have significantly advanced the understanding of N 2 ER in aqueous solution; however, most have focused on thermodynamic and/or kinetic analyses to elucidate reaction mechanisms, while orbital‐level insights remain largely unexplored. Here, we combine DFT calculations with intrinsic bond orbital analysis to examine orbital evolution during 13 protonation steps of N 2 ER. This approach identifies the orbitals responsible for proton accommodation in each intermediate. We find that nine of the 13 steps involve nitrogen lone‐pair orbitals. These results suggest that protonation kinetics in aqueous N 2 ER are strongly influenced by interactions between nitrogen lone pairs and the local solvation environment, including cations and hydrogen bonding. Moreover, surface modifications, which profoundly affect the reactivity of the metal–nitrogen σ bond but have a lesser influence on nitrogen lone‐pair orbitals are not expected to have a direct impact on the protonation kinetics of N 2 ER. Thus, rational manipulation of the local electrochemical environment, rather than solely modifying the catalyst surface, may be essential for improving N 2 ER performance.

10.1002/celc.70328.abstract: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) has emerged as a powerful fabrication strategy for the design of advanced electrocatalysts for water electrolysis. Owing to its sequential self‐limiting surface reactions, ALD enables atomic‐scale control over film thickness, composition, morphology, and interface structure, while simultaneously providing highly conformal coatings on complex and porous substrates. These characteristics make ALD particularly attractive for engineering electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER), where catalyst utilization, stability, and interface properties critically influence electrochemical performance. Beyond catalyst synthesis, ALD has also emerged as a powerful platform for disentangling structure‐activity‐stability relationships in electrocatalysis. This review discusses recent advances in ALD‐enabled electrocatalyst fabrication for water electrolysis, with emphasis on noble‐metal and earth‐abundant catalyst systems, including transition‐metal oxides, sulfides, and phosphides. Attention is given to the role of ALD in controlling catalyst dispersion, stabilizing active phases, tuning oxidation states, and engineering catalyst–support interactions. In addition, recent developments in interface engineering, ultrathin overlayers, and phase‐controlled oxide systems are highlighted. Finally, current limitations associated with scalability, throughput, and processing cost are discussed together with future perspectives involving spatial ALD (SALD), plasma‐enhanced ALD (PEALD), and operando characterization approaches for next‐generation water electrolysis technologies.

10.1002/cnl2.70210.abstract: ABSTRACT The electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) is considered a promising approach to sustainable ammonia production compared with the Haber–Bosch process. However, eNRR remains significantly hindered by the extreme stability of the N≡N bond, slow proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET), and the kinetically favored hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which collectively reduce ammonia yield and Faradaic efficiency. MXenes represent a unique class of 2D transition‐metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, distinguished by chemically versatile transition‐metal active sites, defect‐rich structures, tunable surface terminations, and metallic conductivity. These properties enable unprecedented tuning of N 2 adsorption, interfacial charge redistribution, orbital hybridization, and adsorption energetics, enabling selective N 2 activation while minimizing competing proton reduction. This review provides a critical overview of the design principles of MXene‐based electrocatalysts for selective ammonia synthesis. The distinctive contribution of this review is to systematically link MXene composition, vacancy engineering, heteroatom doping, single‐atom anchoring, and assembling MXene heterostructures to their effects on electronic structure, adsorption free‐energy landscapes, NRR pathways, and HER suppression. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding catalytic selectivity in terms of the underlying mechanism and structure–activity relationships, derived through advanced operando characterization, density functional theory, and emerging machine‐learning‐assisted catalyst discovery.

10.1002/cphc.70594.abstract: Uranium nitrides UN 2− x are excellent candidates as catalyst for ammonia synthesis, as demonstrated by their historical precedent. However, despite their potential, uranium nitrides have not been extensively investigated. In this study, we theoretically investigated the bulk and surface properties of pure and defective UN 2 (UN 1.75 ) implementing DFT + U approach. Uranium nitride UN 2 is not stable, and vacancies are spontaneously formed leading to N/U ratio between 1.7 and 1.8 depending on the synthesis conditions. The vacancy formation energy of UN 2 was calculated as −0.70 eV. To identify the most stable surface, surface energy was calculated for both UN 2 and UN 1.75 catalyst built in four Miller indices (100), (110), (111), and (121). It was found that (111) surface is the most stable one. Moreover, considering differences in distribution of vacancies in UN 1.75 , a random vacancy distribution for (111) surface shows the lower surface energy of 0.51 J.m −2 . The surface can easily be covered by layer of oxygen at very low oxygen pressure even at high temperature of 1500 K. However, the regeneration of the initial deoxygenated surface is possible under reaction conditions, (N 2 /H 2 ; 1:3) at 1000 K temperature. Regeneration is further facilitated in the presence of ammonia in the gas mixture.

10.1002/cssc.71182.abstract: The commercialization of Zn metal anodes is constrained by dendrite growth and severe side reactions, despite their low cost and high volumetric capacity. Herein, we leverage the microwave‐induced skin effect to establish the hybrid interphase layer by sequentially incorporating Zn 2+ ‐affinitive Cu and HER‐suppressive Bi. The in situ formed protective layer, composed of core–satellite nanoarchitectonics, exhibits a thin and gradient feature owing to the limited penetration depth of electromagnetic energy via ultrafast Joule heating. The introduction of Cu species evolves into CuZn 5 alloy microsphere cores, which bond intimately to the Zn substrate with minimum lattice mismatch, thereby facilitating uniform Zn nucleation and dense deposition. Meanwhile, the confined growth of nanosized Bi satellites effectively suppresses parasitic reactions, endowing the Zn anode with a prolonged lifespan exceeding 3400 h at 5 mA cm −2 . The full cell employing the modified Zn anode and NaV 3 O 8 cathode demonstrates excellent capacity retention of 86% after 1000 cycles at 2 A g −1 .

10.1002/smll.76156.abstract: ABSTRACT Adaptive thermal regulation across diurnal and seasonal cycles remains a critical challenge for energy‐efficient buildings. A switchable dual‐mode Janus‐structured composite is developed by integrating a polyoxymethylene fiber/acrylate resin/BaSO 4 aerogel cooling layer with a graphene aerogel/paraffin wax (PW) phase‐change composite heating layer to achieve synergistic passive radiative cooling, solar‐Joule heating, and latent‐heat storage. The heating layer exhibits high thermal conductivity, high solar‐to‐latent heat conversion efficiency, high latent heat capacity, and high electrical conductivity. This permits a maximum sub‐ambient temperature rise of 17.4°C across the day. The cooling layer delivers a solar reflectivity of 96.2%, a mid‐infrared emissivity of 94.0%, and a low thermal conductivity of 0.053 W m −1 K −1 , achieving a maximum sub‐ambient temperature drop of 21.3°C and a genuine radiative net cooling power of 110.4 W m −2 , with an additional transient thermal buffering provided by the latent heat of PW (239.7 J g −1 ). Outdoor tests verify diurnal regulation and paraffin‐induced temperature hysteresis. Building energy simulations across 15 Chinese cities demonstrate annual energy savings exceeding 10.8% in most regions, with reductions of 9.5 and 15.1 MJ m −2 in heating and cooling demands, respectively. This work provides an effective strategy for all‐weather thermal management and sustainable energy savings under diverse climatic conditions.

10.1002/smll.76214.abstract: ABSTRACT Constructing multiphase heterojunctions endowed with high‐density defects and asymmetric charge distributions is a promising strategy for highly efficient microwave absorption. However, protracted thermodynamic synthesis inherently drives materials toward a low‐energy equilibrium state, triggering interfacial thermal relaxation and defect annihilation that severely deplete active polarization centers. To overcome these thermodynamic constraints, we develop a fast Joule heating strategy combined with in situ selenization to precisely regulate the continuous Co–Se phase evolution pathway. By delivering a non‐equilibrium thermal shock within seconds, this process dynamically arrests the intermediate state of phase evolution, thereby retaining electronically asymmetric, metastable Co 3 Se 4 /CoSe/NC heterojunctions. Bypassing interfacial thermal relaxation, this kinetically frozen structure preserves abundant unrelaxed defects and induces profound localized electron rearrangement, generating potent interfacial polarization centers. This kinetic trapping enhances localized dielectric loss while achieving a moderate degree of graphitization within the carbon matrix for ideal macroscopic impedance matching. Consequently, the optimized composite achieves an outstanding minimum reflection loss of −70.01 dB at a thickness of only 1.5 mm, alongside a broad effective absorption bandwidth of 5.79 GHz at 1.7 mm. This work goes beyond the constraints of traditional thermodynamic synthesis by establishing a non‐equilibrium phase‐engineering approach, thereby creating new possibilities for developing electromagnetic microwave absorption materials.
10.1002/smll.76214.title: Maximizing Polarization Responses in Non‐Equilibrium Heterostructures via Fast Joule Heating for Highly Efficient Microwave Absorption

10.1002/smll.76353.abstract: ABSTRACT Methanol production by carbon dioxide hydrogenation is a promising route for supplying industrial fuel demands, but achieving high methanol selectivity remains challenging due to competing favorable reactions. Here, we investigate model Au/In 2 O 3‐x /TiO 2 (110) catalysts to elucidate the roles of metal‐oxide and oxide‐oxide interactions in CO 2 conversion. Using a combination of ambient‐pressure X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (AP‐XPS), temperature‐programmed desorption (TPD), and catalytic measurements, we show that small coverages of Au (<0.15 monolayer) dispersed on In 2 O 3‐x /TiO 2 (110) significantly enhance both CO 2 and H 2 activation at low temperatures (300–400 K). The Au/In 2 O 3‐x /TiO 2 (110) systems exhibit superior catalytic performance, with the highest methanol selectivity (∼80–85%) and increased conversion rates compared to In 2 O 3‐x /TiO 2 (110) and Au/TiO 2 (110). Spectroscopic results showed that Au nanoparticles promote the formation of oxygen vacancies and enhance CO 2 activation, without inducing the dissociation of methoxy and methanol. Reaction studies support a formate‐mediated reaction pathway, distinct from the CO‐mediated route observed on Au/TiO 2 catalysts that leads to very low methanol selectivity. Oxide‐oxide interactions stabilized the partially reduced In 2 O 3‐x , and prevented Au‐In alloy formation under CO 2 +H 2 conditions, preserving methanol selectivity. These findings highlight the importance of synergistic metal↔oxide‐oxide interactions when designing efficient catalysts for selective hydrogenation of CO 2 to methanol while minimizing the content of Au and In 2 O 3‐x .

10.1002/sus2.70103.abstract: ABSTRACT Solar‐driven photocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (p‐NRR) offers a sustainable pathway for ammonia synthesis under ambient conditions. However, its efficiency is fundamentally hampered by the kinetic inertness of the N≡N triple bond. Herein, we construct oxygen‐vacancy‐induced asymmetric Co 2+ –Ov–Co 3+ units within two‐dimensional (2D) ultrathin LaCoO 3− x nanosheets to address this challenge. Oxygen‐vacancy‐induced symmetry breaking reconstructs the Co–O coordination field, forming Co 2+ sites with redistributed 3d energy levels that strongly couple with π* orbitals of N 2 . In situ spectroscopic measurements and theoretical calculations reveal that these asymmetric sites promote directional electron injection, stabilize the key *NNH intermediate, and decrease the transition‐state energy barrier of the rate‐determining step from 1.98 to 1.38 eV. Moreover, spin‐resolved orbital reconfiguration and orbital‐level modulation further guide the reaction pathway from the conventional distal pathway toward a more thermodynamically favorable alternating mechanism. Consequently, the optimized LaCoO 3− x exhibits a photocatalytic NH 3 production rate of 462.6 µg g −1 h −1 , which is 7.7 times higher than that of pristine LaCoO 3 . This work provides a fundamental insight into orbital‐level catalyst design for highly efficient p‐NRR.

10.1007/s10163-026-02749-3.abstract: Abstract Excess nitrogen in high-strength wastewater represents an environmental burden and an untapped resource for recovery. Conventional nitrogen recovery processes, including ammonia stripping, anammox, and struvite precipitation, require ammonium-rich streams. This study evaluates the potential of an anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) as a platform for wastewater treatment, energy recovery, and retention of ammonium (NH 4 ⁺–N) in the permeate. A 340-d trial was conducted with synthetic wastewater across six sequential operating periods with hydraulic retention times (HRTs) of 3–5 d and influent ammonium concentrations of 1170–2800 mg NH 4 ⁺–N L⁻¹. Under the baseline condition (5-d HRT; 1170 mg NH 4 ⁺–N L⁻¹), the reactor achieved 98% COD removal, 90% ammonium retention, and methane production of 0.28 L CH 4 g COD⁻¹ d⁻¹. At a 3-d HRT or at higher influent ammonium concentrations, process stability declined, with lower COD removal and ammonium retention accompanied by volatile fatty acid accumulation. Descriptive microbial profiles showed enrichment of stress-tolerant taxa and a shift from acetoclastic to hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. The principal contribution is therefore the long-term operational evidence that an AnMBR can produce an ammonium-rich, solids-free permeate that may serve as a feed for downstream nitrogen-recovery processes, while defining the operational conditions associated with stable performance.

10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c01663.abstract: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a van der Waals material with excellent insulating properties that make it well-suited as a gate dielectric in 2D electronic devices. In recent years, the discovery of an ever-increasing list of properties has led to a much broader range of potential applications, including quantum photonics, memristive devices, and extreme-environment coatings. However, current growth methods for hBN films are characterized by a narrow selection of substrates and high temperatures that require transfer and limit scale-up. Here, we report a remote plasma-activated approach to directly synthesize large-area hBN films on a diverse range of representative metallic, semiconducting, and amorphous insulating substrates. Specifically, we employ the spatial afterglow of an Ar/H2 plasma to activate ammonia borane, which enables the growth of thick (>30 nm), uniform, and stoichiometric films on substrates such as Si, SiO2, glass, fused silica, Mo, and Al. Systematic spectroscopic characterization reveals that hBN films can be grown as low as 300 °C. Furthermore, plasma afterglow-grown hBN films exhibit mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties on par with or exceeding those reported by alternate synthesis methods. These results establish plasma afterglow growth for the direct integration of hBN into a wide range of emerging technologies.

10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c02250.abstract: Abstract The AtomicLimits ALD/ALE database is a community resource that catalogues atomic layer deposition (ALD) and atomic layer etching (ALE) processes reported in the literature. While widely used, it currently captures only a small fraction of the available information, with limited process information per entry, and relies on manual curation. As ALD/ALE process development grows in demand and complexity, with many interdependent parameters and increasingly sophisticated chemistries such as for multicomponent films, decades of experimental and simulation knowledge remain locked across publications, supplementary files, and lab notebooks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs), offer a path to unlock this knowledge for data-driven analysis and process design, but realizing this potential depends on structured, machine-readable data. In this perspective, we propose a framework to evolve AtomicLimits into an AI-ready knowledge infrastructure that integrates literature-extracted, experimental, and simulation data through a community-defined schema, a structured template that specifies which data fields to capture and how to organize them. We outline the AI capabilities this enables, from structured querying to autonomous experimentation, and discuss the coordinated community effort required to realize this vision for the atomic-scale processing field.

10.1021/acs.energyfuels.6c03763.abstract: Abstract Practical direct air capture (DAC) demands a sorbent contactor that simultaneously delivers high active-material loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid regeneration─requirements that conventional sorbent architectures rarely satisfy together. Here, we present a woven fiber contactor that addresses these requirements by interlacing dry-fabricated zeolite Y/PTFE fibers with copper wire supports into a structured contactor. Compared to a stacked laminate configuration, the woven sorbent exhibited markedly more efficient mass transfer, yielding a narrower mass transfer zone (LMTZ = 4.4 mm and 11.1 mm at 50 sccm) and a steeper breakthrough front. This structural advantage translated into robust sorption performance, with CO2 capture capacity varying by only 11.7% across a 10-fold increase in feed flow rate (50–500 sccm, corresponding to superficial velocities 5.79 × 10–3 to 5.79 × 10–2 m/s) compared to 19.2% for the stacked laminate. The woven architecture further reduced pressure drop by 7- to 18-fold over a wide range of superficial velocities (1.16 × 10–2–5.79 × 10–1 m/s). The integrated copper wires enabled electrified temperature swing adsorption (e-TSA) with near-instantaneous heating, driving CO2 desorption within 1 min. Over 10 consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles, the module retained an average capacity of 1.01 mmol/gsorbent with less than 6.93% variance. Together, these results establish the woven fiber contactor as a scalable platform that unites high sorbent loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid electrified regeneration for energy-efficient DAC.

Herein, we systematically synthesized and benchmarked Ru catalysts supported on RE (=Gd, La, and Sm)-modified CeO2 under identical conditions to establish promoter-structure–activity relationships. Rare-earth incorporation increased the Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio, oxygen-vacancy concentration, and weak acidic sites, facilitating electron transfer to Ru, promoting N2 activation, and potentially facilitating interfacial hydrogen spillover. H2-TPD suggested improved hydrogen mobility and utilization at the Ru/CeO2 interface. These findings establish Gd as the most effective promoter for Ru/CeO2 under mild synthesis conditions.

10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c04121.abstract: Abstract Microwave-driven carbothermal shock (CTS) synthesis has attracted considerable attention as an ultrafast route for nanomaterial production. However, controlling nanoparticle nucleation and growth during the extremely short microwave irradiation period remains challenging. Although defect-rich carbon materials have frequently been employed in microwave-driven CTS synthesis, the influence of a separately introduced defect-containing surface layer on nanoparticle formation remains insufficiently understood. In this study, carbon cloth (CC) was coated with a polyacrylonitrile (PAN) solution and thermally oxidized at 200–400 °C to modify the surface carbon structure through the evolution of PAN-derived polyaromatic clusters prior to microwave irradiation. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated that increasing the oxidation temperature promoted the formation of larger and more ordered polyaromatic domains, accompanied by changes in the surface defect characteristics. These structural variations were associated with distinct Cu nanoparticle sizes and distributions following CTS synthesis. Among the investigated oxidation temperatures, the PAN-coated CC treated at 300 °C produced the smallest and most uniformly dispersed Cu nanoparticles, with an average diameter of 58 ± 25 nm. These findings suggest that controlling the structural evolution of PAN-derived surface carbon layers can provide a practical approach for regulating nanoparticle size and dispersion during microwave-driven CTS synthesis.

10.1021/acsaem.6c01593.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (ENRR) is an environmentally friendly and sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) production. It offers a promising alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, significantly reducing its environmental impact. In this study, cobalt hydroxide nanoneedle arrays were successfully prepared on nickel foam (Co(OH)2@NF) by a facile hydrothermal approach. The Co(OH)2 structure was then overlayered simply by Au atoms through galvanic replacement. This process created a synergistic effect between Co and Au, which promotes N2 activation while suppressing the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that Au incorporation significantly modifies the electron density redistribution around adsorbed N2 molecules, creating more favorable sites for protonation and thereby enhancing the ENRR kinetics. The replacement of Co with Au atoms increased the Faradaic efficiency (FE) from 38.2 ± 2.4% to 90.1 ± 2.3%. The NH3 yield rate (rNH3) nearly doubled from 0.45 µg h−1 cm−2 ± 0.02 (2.00 × 10−8 mol h−1 cm−2) at –0.15 V vs RHE to 0.85 ± 0.06 µg h−1 cm−2 (4.98 × 10−8 mol h−1 cm−2) at a more favorable potential of + 0.00 V vs RHE. The Co(OH)2–Au@NF electrocatalyst can be used as a stable and effective electrocatalyst for the green synthesis of NH3, which is, to the best of our knowledge, among the highest FE values reported for ENRR under ambient conditions, particularly considering the extremely low overpotential.

10.1021/acsaem.6c02542.abstract: Abstract Modulation of the electric double layer (EDL) by different alkali metal cations (AMCs) is a powerful yet poorly understood strategy for steering the selectivity of the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) over the dominant hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) for ammonia synthesis. This study unveils a transformative mechanism for steering the selectivity of the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) over the dominant hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the charged Cu(111)/water interface using constant-potential ab initio molecular dynamics. This study examines the alkali metal cations (Li+, Na+, and K+) modulated proton dynamics near the electrified interface at –0.5 V vs RHE. The core discovery goes beyond the traditional spectator-ion paradigm by establishing a dynamic solvation descriptor. The results demonstrate that while Li+ remains trapped in the outer Helmholtz plane (OHP) due to a rigid hydration shell, K+ undergoes spontaneous partial desolvation, migrating into the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). This dynamic relocation provides direct electrostatic stabilization of the critical *NNH intermediate, lowering its activation barrier to 0.973 eV—a pathway inaccessible with Li+ or Na+. Furthermore, the presence of K+ in the IHP induces a catastrophic disruption of the interfacial hydrogen-bond network. By forcing an H-down water orientation, K+ physically deconstructs the proton-transfer pathways required for the competing HER. While Li+ and Na+ maintain multiple water orientations that promote hydrogen bonding, the steric gating effect of K+ effectively suppresses HER. These atomistic insights are consistent with experimental findings showing high NH3 Faradaic efficiency in KOH at –0.5 V vs RHE. By correlating cation desolvation kinetics with proton steric gating, this work identifies hydration-shell lability and local-field effects as the fundamental drivers of selectivity, offering a sophisticated roadmap for designing electrified liquid interfaces for sustainable ammonia synthesis.

10.1021/acsami.6c12867.abstract: Abstract Traditional metal heat sinks are limited by moderate thermal conductivity, high density, and poor flexibility, which restrict their use in compact and lightweight electronics. Graphene films offer high in-plane thermal conductivity, but rapid reduction of graphene oxide (GO) releases gases from oxygen-containing groups and can generate pores, interlayer damage, and poor film densification. Here, we report a precursor-design strategy that combines reduced graphene oxide nanosheets (GNs) with carboxylated cellulose nanofibers (CNFs). The composite films (GO/GNs-X) were prepared by blade coating, hot-press carbonization, and secondary Joule-heating graphitization. The combined precursor was designed to mitigate gas-release-induced damage and support carbon-network reconstruction during high-temperature treatment. The optimized GF, with a thickness of approximately 25 μm, reached an in-plane thermal conductivity of 950.5 ± 20 W m–1 K–1 and an electrical conductivity of 2.31 × 105 S m–1. At a comparable thickness, this thermal conductivity was 26.6% higher than that of an additive-free RGO-2600-ref film prepared without GNs/CNF modification. In LED heat-dissipation tests, the surface-centre temperature decreased from 83.7 to 40.4 °C. Because individual-additive controls were not included, the respective contributions of GNs and CNF could not be separated. These results establish combined precursor modification as a route to thin, lightweight graphene heat spreaders. Such films may be useful for thermal management in compact electronics, foldable devices, and aerospace systems.

10.1021/acsanm.6c04223.abstract: Abstract This study reports the continuous hydrothermal synthesis of Mg-doped Co3O4 spinel nanomaterials in supercritical water. By optimizing the synthesis parameters, crystalline MgxCo3−xO4 nanospinels (22−35 nm) were obtained directly at 391 °C with τ ≥ 0.1 s and a Mg/Co ratio of 0.25, without thermal post-treatment. Under these conditions, the formation of secondary (Mg,Co)(OH)2 phases was suppressed. Structural refinement indicates a moderately inverse spinel lattice, with Mg2+ incorporation limited to x ≤ 0.24, consistent with the formation of a thermodynamically stable Mg0.24Co2.76O4 spinel phase, as confirmed by HAADF-STEM-EDX analysis. Furthermore, the mixed oxides were evaluated as catalyst precursors for ammonia decomposition after reduction in H2 at 600 °C to generate active metallic cobalt particles embedded in a MgO matrix. Catalytic studies revealed that the performance is determined by a balance between reducibility and cobalt dispersion. On the one hand, increasing Mg content decreases the extent of reduction of the precursor, leading to a lower fraction of metallic cobalt in the catalyst. On the other hand, higher Mg concentrations improve the dispersion of metallic Co0 and its interaction within the MgO matrix, thereby suppressing metal particle sintering. This study demonstrates that precise control of the synthesis enables a detailed understanding of the phase formation in Co−Mg mixed oxides and establishes a reliable strategy for the continuous synthesis of catalyst precursors that yield highly efficient, sintering-resistant catalysts.

10.1021/acscatal.6c03505.abstract: Abstract Commercialization of electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) is hindered by limited catalyst performance, the lack of scalable electrochemical cell architectures, and an incomplete understanding of performance-limiting processes. This work aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of catalyst composition and microstructure, device configuration, and reaction mechanisms. Molybdenum (Mo) metal single atoms and clusters supported on mesoporous nitrogen-doped carbon were synthesized with tunable pore sizes via a five-second photothermal pyrolysis of a self-assembled bottlebrush block copolymer (BBCP) template. For eNRR, improved Mo dispersion enhanced electrochemical accessibility, while the coexistence of atomically dispersed Mo species and Mo clusters produced a structurally heterogeneous catalytic environment that benefits eNRR. A gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) flow cell was constructed for continuous operation testing; the catalyst–device system achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 21.6% and an ammonia yield rate of 34.7 μg h–1 mg–1. Intermediate pore sizes and balanced electrode wettability promoted effective triple-phase boundary formation and active-site utilization. Electrochemical characterization combined with machine-learning analysis of flow-cell parameters indicated that activation polarization is the dominant loss mechanism, governed primarily by intrinsic active-site kinetics and electrochemically accessible surface area. In contrast, pore size, metal dispersion, and electrode wettability primarily regulate site accessibility rather than mass-transport limitations. Together, these results provide a framework linking catalyst structure, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations in eNRR flow-cell systems and offer practical design guidelines for advancing scalable eNRR technology.

10.1021/acscatal.6c05587.abstract: Abstract Hetero-anion doping has emerged as an effective approach to modulate the physicochemical and catalytic properties of perovskite-type oxides. In this study, nanosized CeO2 synthesized by a continuous flow-type supercritical hydrothermal synthesis (SHS) process was employed as a precursor for a solid-state reaction with Ba(NH2)2, enabling the low-temperature synthesis of single-phase perovskite oxynitride–hydride BaCeO3–xNyHz (BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS) with a high surface area and abundant N3– and H– species. Ru-loaded BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS exhibited a maximum ammonia synthesis rate of 9.0 mmol g–1 h–1 at 300 °C and 0.9 MPa and showed up to a 6-fold enhancement in activity compared with the corresponding Ru/BaCeO3–xNyHz prepared from commercial CeO2, owing to the enhanced generation of anion vacancies at the Ru–support interface. Moreover, BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS acted as a highly efficient support for various transition metals in ammonia synthesis and for Ni in ammonia decomposition, achieving >99% conversion at 560 °C with a low apparent activation energy (75 kJ mol–1). These findings demonstrate that enhancing the solid-state reactivity of oxide precursors through nanoscale engineering provides a general strategy for the low-temperature synthesis of highly active hetero-anion perovskite catalysts for ammonia synthesis and decomposition.

10.1021/acscatal.6c07016.abstract: Abstract Ammonia synthesis under mild conditions remains challenging because of the inertness of the N≡N bond and the limited ability of conventional catalysts to couple efficient dinitrogen activation with rapid hydrogenation. Here, we report a LiH/FePcG catalyst in which strong interfacial coupling between LiH and Fe–N–C sites enable efficient ammonia synthesis. Comprehensive characterization, including structural analysis, kinetic study, isotopic-labelling, gas-phase mass spectrometry, and in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) reveal that the catalytic activity originates from interfacial active sites. Under reaction conditions, structural nitrogen atoms within the Fe–Nx moieties undergo reversible consumption and reconstruction, demonstrating the dynamic participation of the Fe–N–C framework in ammonia synthesis. Concurrently, hydridic hydrogen supplied by LiH directly participates in the initial hydrogenation steps, while the LiH/Fe–N–C interface generates Fe-centered multicomponent hydride species essential for N2 binding and activation. An inverse H/D kinetic isotope effect, an H2-promoted 28N2/30N2 exchange rate, in situ spectroscopic evidence, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations collectively support a non-classical, hydrogen-assisted pathway for dinitrogen activation rather than the conventional direct N≡ bond cleavage. These findings establish interfacial hydride chemistry as a cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis and provide a strategy for designing advanced catalysts under mild conditions.

10.1021/acsenergylett.6c02477.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical ammonia synthesis via a lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) faces a fundamental selectivity challenge in which proton donors that accelerate productive protonation simultaneously promote parasitic hydrogen evolution. Here, we demonstrate that 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE), an amphiphilic alcohol, mitigates this limitation by decoupling thermodynamic acidity from kinetic reactivity. Despite its high acidity, TFE suppresses parasitic reactions through rapid interfacial passivation associated with its fluorinated structure, while modulating the microstructure of a fluoride-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Blending TFE with ethanol further optimizes proton activity and hydrogen bonding, yielding a thin, uniform SEI enriched in highly crystalline LiF with reduced interfacial resistance. The optimized electrolyte achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 59.0% in a continuous-flow reactor, maintained stable performance under potential-cycling, and reached 82.8% in a high-pressure batch reactor. This study highlights proton-donor engineering as a key strategy to modulate the SEI nanostructure for selectivity in Li-NRR.

10.1021/acsmaterialslett.6c00756.abstract: Abstract The recent discovery of molybdenum oxynitride (MoO2–x/Mo2N) being an effective plasmonic catalyst demonstrated potential for light-driven ammonia synthesis under ambient pressure. However, its preparation requires high-temperature ammonia annealing to introduce lattice nitrogen, increasing both cost and process complexity. Here, we investigate molybdenum oxide (MoO3–x), the precursor to synthesize MoO2–x/Mo2N, as a catalyst for ammonia synthesis. We show that molybdenum oxide undergoes continuous nitrogen incorporation during the reaction, accompanied by enhanced catalytic activity. Time-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals the emergence of nitrogen-containing surface environments. Thermal treatment is sufficient to induce this evolution, which approaches a relatively stable state after several hours. Notably, both molybdenum oxide and pre-synthesized MoO2–x/Mo2N develop similar nitrogen-containing surface chemical environments under reaction conditions. These findings demonstrate that the catalyst surface dynamically evolves during ammonia synthesis and that nitrogen incorporation is closely associated with enhanced catalytic activity.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c06287.abstract: Abstract Developing effective electrocatalysts that can convert low-concentration nitrate (NO3–) into ammonia (NH3) in dilute electrolytes remains a major challenge. In this work, high-performance atomically dispersed CuCo catalysts (CuCo-ADCs) were prepared using a hydrothermal route. When tested in electrolyte containing 50 ppm NO3–-N and 5 mM K2SO4 (supporting electrolyte), the catalyst delivered a high NH3 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 92.15%, ammonia selectivity of 96.33%, and NH3 production rate of 281.28 μg h–1 cm–2 at –0.6 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Electrochemical measurements indicated reduced solution diffusion resistance for this catalyst. After 10 h of continuous operation, more than 85% of the initial catalytic activity could be retained. Mechanistic characterizations suggested that the atomic-level dispersion accelerated reaction kinetics and suppressed the competing hydrogen evolution reaction. Such improvement originated from the optimized *NO3 adsorption and decreased N═O bond dissociation energy through bimetallic synergy. Within this catalytic system, Cu drove the nitrate reduction reaction, Co was responsible for key bond cleavage, and Ni promoted hydrogenation steps as well as product desorption. This study offers alternative design ideas for atomically dispersed catalysts intended for resource recovery from low-concentration nitrate-rich wastewater. The present catalytic system may be applied for simultaneous nitrogen removal and ammonia generation in practical wastewater treatment.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c08592.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical transformation of nitrate (NO3–) into ammonia (NH3) offers an environmentally sustainable pathway to complete the nitrogen cycle, enabling both green NH3 synthesis and NO3– pollution remediation. Herein, we propose an in situ synergistic reconstruction strategy for fabricating a Cu2O@Co-carbon nanofibers (CNFs) pre-electrocatalyst, integrated with the glycerol oxidation reaction (GOR) to replace the energy-intensive oxygen evolution reaction (OER), thereby significantly reducing energy consumption toward electrocatalytic NO3–-to-NH3 conversion. The potential-dependent reconstruction gives rise to coexisting Co0 and Co(OH)2 species together with active Cu sites. Electrochemical measurements and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support their complementary roles in *H generation and NO3– activation, respectively, thereby promoting the NO3RR while suppressing competing reactions. The resulting catalyst delivers an exceptional NH3 yield rate of 61.0 mg cm–2 h–1 at industrial-level current density, manifesting outstanding catalytic performance. This study offers a novel design principle and a reliable strategy for developing high-efficiency non-noble-metal-based bifunctional electrocatalysts and advanced coupled electrochemical systems.

10.1021/jacs.6c06380.abstract: Abstract Ba3AlO4-xNyHz with an antiperovskite structure is employed as a support for transition-metal catalysts for ammonia synthesis. This metastable material is synthesized by employing multiple anions with different valences and ionic radii. The optimized non-noble metal catalyst, Co(5.8 wt %)/Ba3AlO4-xNyHz/Al2O3, exhibits an exceptional ammonia synthesis rate of 15.9 mmol g–1 h–1 at 0.9 MPa and 300 °C, outperforming benchmark Cs–Ru/MgO, industrial Fe catalyst, and recently reported non-noble metal catalysts. Structural analyses show that Ba3AlO4-xNyHz and Co species self-organize on γ-Al2O3 nanorods to form a hierarchically structured catalyst. Combined experimental and density functional theory analyses reveal that the high activity originates from incorporated (N2)− ions at Co–Ba–Al interfacial sites, where the combination of Ba and Al plays distinct roles in N2 activation and NHx formation, respectively. These findings not only provide a strategy for stabilizing metastable crystal structures through the incorporation of diverse anionic species but also demonstrate a unique cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis mediated by highly activated molecular (N2)− ions.

10.1021/jacs.6c18484.abstract: Abstract Ammonia, an emerging energy carrier, demands advanced catalysts for synthesis under mild conditions to integrate with green hydrogen. We herein establish a family of metal fluoride supports (MFn, M = Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, or Ba) as a tunable “all-in-one” platform for ruthenium (Ru) catalysts. These Ru/MFn systems unify the critical merits of various existing catalysts, such as support-mediated activation of reactants and air stability. Varying the host cation can direct the catalytic pathway. Consequently, Ru/NaF exhibits excellent turnover frequency, while Ru/BaF2 delivers an NH3 synthesis rate of 58.0 mmolNH3 gcat–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 0.9 MPa─surpassing all reported Ru-based catalysts with ≤4 wt % Ru and without external promoters. Advanced characterization reveals that the fluorine vacancy formation energies of the alkali and alkaline-earth lattices, together with the vacancy-reactant interactions, dictate the divergent catalytic mechanisms mediated by different active sites. This work expands the chemistry of metal fluorides, launching a new paradigm for potentially viable NH3-synthesis under mild conditions.

10.1021/jacsau.6c01238.abstract: Abstract Driven by the growing need for sustainable ammonia production and effective nitrate remediation, the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has emerged as a promising technology. This process enables the conversion of nitrate pollutants into ammonia under mild operating conditions, offering a greener alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch route. However, the complex multielectron and multiproton transfer pathways involved in NO3RR require catalysts capable of precisely regulating intermediate adsorption, activation, and transformation. Atomically precise metal nanoclusters (NCs), with their well-defined atomic structures, tunable electronic properties, and identifiable active sites, have recently attracted considerable attention as model catalysts for elucidating structure–activity relationships. This perspective discusses the fundamental aspects of NO3RR, including key intermediates and reaction mechanisms, and summarizes recent advances in the use of atomically precise metal NCs for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. The catalytic performances of mono-, bi-, and trimetallic NCs are systematically compared, highlighting the roles of active-site engineering, ligand modulation, heterometal incorporation, and cluster assembly in regulating activity and selectivity. The perspective concludes by discussing the key challenges that remain in this field and highlighting future research directions toward the development of NC-based electrocatalysts with enhanced activity, selectivity, and long-term stability for sustainable ammonia production.

10.1116/6.0005783.abstract: Phosphorus-containing hybrid organic-inorganic materials demonstrate unique physicochemical properties making them suitable candidates for energy storage, electrocatalysis, and as protective and biocompatible coatings. Of special interest in this regard are metal phosphonate films, where the organic group bound to the P atom can tune functional properties of the films. However, the deposition of such materials in thin-film form remains challenging and has achieved only limited success. In this work, we present two deposition processes employing combination of atomic and molecular layer deposition approaches for the growth of aluminium phosphonates, utilizing trimethylaluminum as the Al source, and dimethyl methylphosphonate and dimethyl phenylphosphonate as the P sources, respectively. Both processes demonstrated saturated growth, and the incorporation of the phosphonate groups was confirmed using ex situ x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. As-grown films demonstrated a P/Al ratio of ca. 0.2–0.3, indicating the formation of a phosphonate-doped alumina matrix. Through density functional theory calculations, we delineated differences in precursor chemistry and their impact on growth characteristics for the processes. These films deposited using these approaches demonstrated superior thermal stability (≥500 °C) and hydrolytic stability under all tested conditions. The findings of this study can inspire the development of efficient processes for the incorporation of organophosphorus groups in such hybrid thin films.

10.1117/12.3114653.abstract: Thermal atomic layer etching (ALE) provides a precise pathway for aluminum surface preparation, optimizing optical performance at vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) wavelengths. This study investigates using trimethylaluminum (TMA) and anhydrous hydrogen fluoride (HF) to remove native aluminum oxide prior to encapsulation with dielectric thin films via atomic layer deposition (ALD). This integrated ALE/ALD process enables high-reflectance coatings and bandpass filters for applications below 200 nm. We demonstrate that the Al2O3 etch rate is highly sensitive to chamber conditioning; specifically, alkali halides like cesium fluoride catalyze the reaction. This effect lowers the thermal threshold for etching from >300 °C to 125 °C, protecting sensitive substrates and minimizing subsurface damage. While deep etching can increase roughness, lower temperatures enhance selectivity for native oxide removal. Consequently, a VUV mirror with ALD MgF2 improves from 60% to 80% reflectivity at 120 nm using this method. We discuss applications in electronics, superconductors, and the scalability of these methods for meter-class mirrors intended for future NASA large-aperture space observatories.

10.1142/s3060932126300076.abstract: Electrochemical ammonia synthesis offers a promising sustainable alternative to the Haber–Bosch process, but progress remains fragmented across catalysis, ammonia validation, and reactor engineering. This review investigates an integrated framework combining catalyst design, reaction mechanisms, analytical validation, and reactor engineering to interlink the activation of nitrogen with consistent ammonia verification for high-yield ammonia synthesis. The roles of electronic structure, defect chemistry, active sites, interfacial effects, and electrolytes promote nitrogen activation and ammonia selectivity and inhibit the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction. Conventional electrochemical nitrogen reduction and alternative pathways, including nitrate and nitrite reduction, plasma-assisted synthesis, and lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction, are critically compared using common performance criteria encompassing reaction mechanisms, ammonia productivity, Faradaic efficiency, energy consumption, stability, and scalability. Specifically, the review pays attention to a critical assessment of ammonia quantification methods, which include colorimetric techniques, ion chromatography, nuclear magnetic resonance, and isotope labeling to reduce errors in ammonia quantification. The review further bridges catalyst-level performance and practical reactor operation by evaluating flow cells, gas-diffusion electrodes, membrane-based and zero-gap configurations, and stack architectures in terms of mass transport, current density, reactant utilization, product separation, and energy efficiency. Finally, this review identifies the energy barriers in the engineering to transition from laboratory scale to scalable ammonia generation.
