10.21203/rs.3.rs-10454878/v1.abstract: Abstract The transition of the lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) toward industrial application remains a formidable challenge. Achieving stable operation under ampere-level current density is particularly pivotal in this regard. An ideal solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) plays a decisive role in determining the overall efficiency and feasibility. Current research predominantly focuses on bulk electrolyte optimization for SEI control, leaving the direct tailoring of electrode interphase underexplored. This lack of fundamental understanding hinders the achievement of highly efficient and stable Li-NRR toward practical application. Here, we report a strategy to atomic-scale restructure the interfacial microenvironment by engineering Cu substrates with a predominant (220) facet, leveraging the crystallographic orientation to present a definitive pathway for stable interphase. The Cu (220) facet selectively promotes the specific adsorption of anions within the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP), establishing a locally concentrated anion microenvironment even within dilute electrolytes. This facet induced enrichment overrides conventional reduction pathways dominated by solvents, triggering a kinetically accelerated evolution of a thin, robust SEI rich in inorganic components composed primarily of LiF and Li 2 S. This tailored interphase architecture enhances the interfacial Li + diffusion coefficient by two orders of magnitude and shortens the N 2 transport pathway, effectively balancing the transport of Li + , N 2 and H + , enabling the system to sustain a remarkable 1.1 µmol s − 1 cm − 2 ammonia production rate at a sustained current density of -500 mA cm − 2 . This work demonstrates that atomic scale manipulation of substrate crystallography can dictate macroscopic interphase chemistry, charting a robust and scalable pathway for high flux electrochemical synthesis.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11284169/v1.abstract: Abstract Rational catalyst design for ammonia decomposition requires navigating coupled structural and electronic effects that govern reaction energetics across a large configurational space. Here, we integrate density functional theory (DFT), microkinetic modeling (MKM), and interpretable machine learning to establish a physics-guided screening framework. For the most active stepped Ru(10–13) surface, MKM identifies NH* dissociation as the rate-limiting step and defines an NH* binding-energy window of -4.47 to -3.84 eV that sustains near-maximal turnover frequency across 673–750 K and applied fields of 0 and − 0.4 V/Å. A DFT database comprising 1,132 Ru and 270 Co configurations spanning surface structure, adatom coverage, and electronic state was used to train a gradient-boosted model, achieving a Ru test mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.082 eV. Although direct Ru-to-Co transfer yields a 0.397 eV error, incorporating only 45 Co configurations reduces the Co test MAE to 0.120 eV. SHAP analysis identifies charge, local site coordination, and surface energy as the dominant factors governing NH* binding. Guided by these relationships, screening ~ 33,000 physically constructed candidates enriches the population within the kinetic target, while constrained-DFT validation supports the model’s ability to identify promising configurations.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11507422/v1.abstract: Abstract Solvent selection can exert a substantial influence on the microstructural development and functional response of oxide thin films prepared by aerosol-based deposition. In this study, nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄) thin films were deposited on glass substrates by nebulizer-assisted spray pyrolysis using water, methanol, ethanol and isopropanol-containing precursor solutions. The resulting films were examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), UV–visible spectroscopy and ammonia (NH₃) sensing measurements. XRD analysis was reported to be consistent with a cubic spinel structure, while the ethanol-containing formulation produced the sharpest diffraction peaks and the largest estimated crystallite size (approximately 24.5 nm). SEM observations indicated a comparatively uniform, porous and less agglomerated surface for the ethanol-derived film. Optical analysis yielded an estimated band gap of approximately 1.86 eV for this sample, lower than the values reported for the water-, methanol- and isopropanol-derived films. The ethanol-derived film also exhibited a concentration-dependent current response to NH₃, with a reported response of approximately 500% at 250 ppm. These findings suggest that solvent composition is a potentially useful processing variable for tailoring the structural, optical and gas-sensing behaviour of spray-pyrolysed NiFe₂O₄ films. Further quantitative validation—including replicate measurements, response and recovery times, selectivity, baseline stability and uncertainty analysis—is required before practical sensor performance can be established.

10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-g53rc/v3.abstract: We report the synthesis of Fe foams by dynamic hydrogen bubble template (DHBT)-assisted electrodeposition and their electrocatalytic performance for the selective reduction of nitrate to ammonia, a strategy that mitigates nitrate pollution while providing a decentralized route for ammonia production. Fe-foam_90s@Ti achieves a Faradaic efficiency of up to 97% and a partial current density for ammonia formation approaching -1 A cm -2 without externally imposed convection. Operando Raman spectroscopy tracked the potential-dependent reduction of surface Fe oxides and, together with identical-location scanning electron microscopy (IL-SEM), supported the assignment of metallic Fe as the catalytically active state for selective ammonia formation. Potential-dependent ICP-MS and ion chromatography analyses identified an operating window with minimal Fe dissolution, in which the corrosion-prone catalyst can be electrochemically stabilized through cathodic protection. The catalyst was further implemented in a laboratory-scale flow-cell electrolyzer under galvanostatic conditions, demonstrating its compatibility with continuous-flow operation. Together, these results establish DHBT-derived Fe foams as promising electrocatalysts for high-rate ammonia electrosynthesis and support their further evaluation in scaled flow-cell systems.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009696/v2.abstract: Selective catalytic conversion of complex hydrocarbons into light olefins remains challenging because of costly catalyst preparation and catalyst deactivation under severe cracking conditions. Here, we report pulsed Joule heating for highly selective light olefin production from complex hydrocarbon mixtures. By precisely regulating reaction severity, this catalyst-free approach achieves light olefin yields comparable to those reported for catalytic cracking. We systematically characterized the feedstock molecular composition and evaluated olefin yields of diverse hydrocarbon mixtures, including polyolefins, crude oils, Fischer-Tropsch wax, and shale oil. To quantify the effects of pulse parameters on olefin production, we developed a spatiotemporal reactor model based on a quasi-molecular reaction network. The model reveals that pulsed Joule heating regulates high-temperature reactions to match product removal, thereby improving olefin yield and selectivity. Guided by the model, catalyst-free pulsed Joule heating crude oil pyrolysis was optimized and achieved a light olefin yield of approximately 38 wt%. These findings establish a quantitative framework for temporal regulation of complex hydrocarbon pyrolysis and provide a basis for industrial electrified olefin production.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009859/v1.abstract: Selective electrochemical conversion of nitrate (NO 3 - ) to dinitrogen (N 2 ) is attractive for nitrate remediation but remains challenging because competing hydrogenation pathways often yield reduced nitrogen products. Here, we develop a self-supported flexible electrified membrane (α-Co/NC@CNTFEM) by integrating phase-defined hexagonal close-packed (HCP) α-Co/nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) into a conductive carbon nanotube (CNT) framework. The resulting membrane combines a uniformly integrated catalytic phase with a thin, interconnected porous architecture suitable for flow-through electrochemical operation. At an initial nitrate concentration of 10 mg L -1 , α-Co/NC@CNT-FEM achieves 96.5% nitrate conversion, 81.5% N 2 Faradaic efficiency, and 97.9% N 2 selectivity, exceeding the corresponding mixed-phase Co NP /NC@CNT-FEM and bare CNT-FEM. The enhanced N 2 selectivity is associated with the coupled effects of the phase-defined α-Co, N-doped carbon matrix, and flow-through CNT microenvironment, which may favor N–N coupling while suppressing excessive hydrogenation. Moreover, our results also reveal that stable nitrate removal on this platform is maintained over 10 consecutive cycles. This work demonstrates crystal-phase engineering coupled with electrified membrane design as a materials strategy for selective nitrate-to-N 2 conversion.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010321/v1.abstract: Direct utilization of dinitrogen (N2) in organic synthesis remains an unmet challenge in sustainable chemistry, particularly under mild conditions. Conventional transition-metal-mediated N2 functionalization typically requires elaborately designed catalysts under harsh conditions, limiting operational practicality. Here, we report a mechanochemical strategy that achieves rapid, lithium-mediated N2 reduction at ambient pressure and temperature in under two minutes, delivering polymorphic mixtures of α- and β-lithium nitride. The resulting metal nitride serves as a versatile platform for single nitrogen-atom transfer: applied to skeletal conversion reactions, it enables direct O-to-N transmutation of furans and aromatic oxonium salts into the corresponding pyrroles and pyridine derivatives, establishing a formal incorporation of N2 into N-heterocycles. The photophysical consequences of the single-atom edit on excited-state properties of the molecular chromophores were evaluated.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010462/v1.abstract: Ammonia borane (NH3BH3) is a hydrogen rich molecular solid whose structural behaviour is governed by molecular orientation and N–H· · ·H–B dihydrogen interactions. Its temperature-dependent phase transition is conventionally described as an order–disorder transition from a disordered tetragonal phase to a more ordered orthorhombic phase. However, this description does not fully capture the underlying local structure. Single crystal X-ray diffraction, X-ray total scattering, Pair Distribution Function (PDF) analysis and Reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) modelling reveal an unexpected inversion of local structural order across the phase transition. At 300 K, despite pronounced disorder in the average tetragonal structure, the local structure exhibits three preferential NH3 orientations, whereas the BH3 groups remain substantially disordered. In contrast, at 100 K, modelling reveals substantial local disorder of NH3 despite the more ordered average orthorhombic structure. Single crystal diffraction additionally reveals weak satellite reflections, while the 100 K powder diffraction pattern is better reproduced by a trial commensurately modulated model with threefold periodicity than by the conventional average structure. Together, these results indicate that the low temperature phase combines periodic structural modulation with substantial local disorder, demonstrating that average and local structural order do not evolve in parallel with temperature.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15010462/v1.title: Structural Order Reversed: Local and Average Structure Across the Ammonia Borane Phase Transition

10.3390/hydrogen7040168.abstract: This study investigates the integration of Haber–Bosch waste-heat recovery with solid oxide electrolysis (SOE) and evaluates its techno-economic implications through the comparison of stand-alone SOE, hybrid SOE–AWE, and stand-alone AWE hydrogen production configurations. The HB synthesis loop was first simulated and analyzed to quantify the residual heat available after internal heat recovery and assess its thermal suitability for SOE steam generation. The recoverable HB heat initially covers 55% of the SOE evaporator duty. Further optimization of the SOE-side heat-exchanger network using Aspen Energy Analyzer V14 increases this coverage to 63%, enabling SOE to thermally support up to 63% of the hydrogen demand. Additional heat integration opportunities identified using Aspen Energy Analyzer (AEA) increase this coverage to 63%, enabling the SOE system to supply up to 63% of the hydrogen demand. The remaining hydrogen production requirement is investigated under two distinct configurations: (i) a stand-alone SOE system with an internal steam generation unit and (ii) a hybrid configuration consisting of 63% SOE and 37% AWE. These SOE-based configurations are evaluated and compared with a conventional alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) system. The energy analysis demonstrates that SOE-based systems significantly reduce overall energy consumption due to their higher electrochemical efficiency and effective utilization of industrial waste heat. The economic assessment yields LCOH values of 3.90, 3.44, and 2.79 $/kg H2 for the stand-alone SOE, hybrid SOE–AWE, and stand-alone AWE configurations, respectively. Sensitivity analysis indicates that reductions in SOE stack cost combined with improvements in stack lifetime can enable the hybrid configuration to achieve an LCOH of 2.79 $/kg H2, reaching cost parity with the baseline AWE configuration and demonstrating its potential as an energy-efficient and economically competitive pathway for green ammonia production.

10.3390/ma19204402.abstract: Metal nanoparticles supported on carbon nanofibers (CNFs) are promising for catalytic and electrochemical applications, but controlling their size, dispersion, and phase during rapid thermal processing remains challenging. Here, we report a dual-solvent microwave carbothermal shock (CTS) method for producing Cu- and Ni-containing nanostructures on CNFs under ambient-pressure conditions. Ethanolic metal nitrate precursors were deposited on pristine CNFs, and hexane was introduced as an antisolvent before microwave irradiation. At 0.05 M Cu(NO3)2, hexane addition decreased the mean Cu-containing particle diameter from 50 ± 20 nm to 33 ± 12 nm and improved dispersion. Varying precursor concentration further altered particle morphology and aggregation. For Ni, single-solvent processing yielded aggregated nanoparticles averaging 43 ± 16 nm, whereas dual-solvent processing produced a dense carbon nanotube network with an apparent mean filament diameter of 20 ± 7 nm. Microscopy and elemental mapping supported the association of Ni-containing particles with the nanotubes. X-ray diffraction identified crystalline face-centered cubic Cu and Ni, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated oxidized surface species. Hexane may additionally supply carbon during Ni-assisted nanotube growth, although its contribution requires confirmation. This approach provides a rapid, tunable route to supported metal nanoparticles and hierarchical carbon nanostructures without continuous external inert or hydrocarbon gas flow.

10.3390/sci8100295.abstract: Nitrate contamination of aquatic environments and the high energy and carbon intensity of conventional ammonia production represent two major and increasingly interconnected sustainability challenges. Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3RR) provides a compelling opportunity to address both by converting a widespread nitrogen pollutant into a value-added chemical and potential energy carrier under comparatively mild conditions. However, practical NO3RR remains constrained by sluggish multistep proton–electron transfer, competing hydrogen evolution, complex nitrogen-containing intermediates, and insufficient control over ammonia selectivity. High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles have recently emerged as a promising catalyst platform for overcoming these limitations because their multielement compositions generate diverse adsorption sites, lattice strain, and tunable electronic interactions that can regulate the binding and transformation of key NO3RR intermediates. This review critically examines the emerging role of HEA nanoparticles in electrocatalytic nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, with emphasis on the relationships among composition, local atomic structure, intermediate adsorption, and catalytic selectivity. Major synthetic strategies, including carbothermal shock, sputtering-based deposition, and wet-chemical co-reduction, are evaluated in terms of their ability to control elemental distribution, particle size, phase stability, and accessible active sites. Particular attention is devoted to mechanistic pathways involving *NO2, *NO, *NHx, and *NH2OH species and to how multimetallic surface environments redirect reaction pathways toward NH3 while suppressing N2, N2O, and H2 formation. Reported Faradaic efficiencies, ammonia production rates, stability, and nitrate-conversion metrics are further benchmarked against conventional monometallic and bimetallic catalysts. Beyond activity under model electrolyte conditions, this review highlights critical knowledge gaps associated with realistic nitrate-contaminated waters, coexisting ions, catalyst reconstruction and metal leaching, long-term stability, energy efficiency, ammonia recovery, and techno-economic scalability. By integrating environmental remediation with decentralized ammonia synthesis, HEA nanoparticles offer a versatile materials framework for advancing nitrate electroreduction toward practically relevant and circular nitrogen-management technologies.

10.5070/rj5.64252.abstract: In order to enhance biochar’s adsorption efficiency for ammonia removal, it must first undergo acid activation, a process in which the surface chemistry of the biochar is altered. Although acid activation is known to increase ammonia adsorption capacity, the effects of specific preparation parameters are not well understood. During activation, biochar is soaked in phosphoric acid and then rinsed to remove residual unbound acid, which could otherwise react with ammonia and interfere with future adsorption measurements. This study focuses on the acid activation step for woodchip biochar pyrolyzed at 500 °C for 15 minutes. Three parameters were investigated: particle size (ground vs. unground), phosphoric acid concentration (15%, 30%, and 45%), and rinsing method (two rinses, five rinses, or a one-hour soak using 20 mL of DI water). pH was measured before and after treatment and used as an indicator of potential ammonia adsorption. To increase readability, the experiment was repeated twice, and samples were prepared at 1 g per condition, resulting in 18 combinations. According to preliminary results, post-activation pH values ranged from 2.2–3.3, whereas initial values ranged from 7.87–9.78. Unground biochar strains consistently showed lower pH values than their ground counterparts, likely due to the difference in particle size. Samples treated with higher acid concentrations (45%) produced lower pH values than those treated with 15% acid, which is consistent with expected trends.

arxiv:2610.15798.abstract: Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is among the most promising techniques to provide hydrogen as both energy carrier and feedstock for the chemical industry, due to its compatibility with intermittent renewable electricity sources. However, a major bottleneck in scaling up PEMWE is the limited supply of the anode catalyst Ir. This work shows a novel approach to tailoring ionomer-free catalyst layers based on custom-made microporous substrates and two different atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes, both using Ir(EtCp)(CHD) precursor. Thermal ALD using O3 as counter-reactant yields mostly metallic Ir/IrOx and an electrode Ir loading of 0.21 mg/cm2. The PEMWE cell-level performance is comparable to a commercial catalyst-coated membrane anode despite 7x lower loading, and is maintained over an accelerated durability test equivalent to 600 h of intermittent operation. Moreover, using a low-loading ALD-made cathode, the total platinum group metal loading is only 0.24 mg/cm2. Plasma-enhanced ALD reduces the Ir loading to 0.04 mg/cm2 by tailoring the catalyst distribution, however, yields lower-activity IrO2. Finally, direct ALD catalyst deposition needs no ionomer-bearing ink. The anodes are therefore compatible with various membrane materials, as demonstrated in a CO2 electrolysis experiment with an anion exchange membrane.
